title: Hantavirus Kills 3 on MV Hondius in Atlantic
excerpt: WHO confirms 8 cases of deadly Andes virus on Dutch expedition ship; 17 American passengers now evacuated to Nebraska.
body:
A deadly outbreak of Andes virus — a rare strain of hantavirus — has claimed three lives aboard the Dutch expedition cruise ship MV Hondius, prompting a coordinated international evacuation and the highest-profile hantavirus response in decades.

**What happened aboard MV Hondius:**
The ship departed Ushuaia, Argentina on April 1, 2026, sailing across the South Atlantic through Antarctica, South Georgia Island, and several remote islands before the crisis escalated. Illness onset among passengers occurred between April 6 and April 28, characterized by fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, and rapid progression to acute respiratory distress. As of May 8, WHO confirmed eight total cases — six laboratory-confirmed — including three deaths, yielding a case fatality ratio of 38%.

**Why Andes virus alarms health officials:**
Unlike most hantaviruses, which spread only through contact with infected rodent urine or droppings, Andes virus is the *only* hantavirus confirmed to transmit person-to-person, typically through close, prolonged contact. That distinction drove heightened concern aboard a ship where the average passenger age is 65. WHO assessed the risk to the global public as low but raised the risk level on the ship itself to moderate. There is no approved antiviral treatment; early intensive supportive care remains the only intervention.

**What the CDC is tracking now:**
All 17 American passengers aboard MV Hondius are now en route to or already at the Nebraska Biocontainment Unit at the University of Nebraska Medical Center. The CDC has issued health guidance to six U.S. states — including Georgia, Arizona, California, Texas, Virginia, and New Jersey — monitoring passengers who disembarked before the outbreak was detected. The 42-day incubation window means new cases remain possible through mid-June.

**What to watch next:**
Health authorities across multiple countries will monitor all former passengers through the full 42-day incubation window, making mid-June the earliest moment the world can exhale on this outbreak.
